{{short description|Distance between probability distributions}}
In computer science, the '''earth mover's distance''' ('''EMD''')<ref name = RTG98>{{Cite book|last1=Rubner|first1=Y.|last2=Tomasi|first2=C.|last3=Guibas|first3=L.J.|title=Sixth International Conference on Computer Vision (IEEE Cat. No.98CH36271) |chapter=A metric for distributions with applications to image databases |chapter-url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1109/iccv.1998.710701|year=1998 |pages=59–66 |publisher=Narosa Publishing House|doi=10.1109/iccv.1998.710701|isbn=81-7319-221-9 |s2cid=18648233 }}</ref> is a measure of dissimilarity between two [[frequency (statistics)|frequency distributions]], [[Probability density function|densities]], or [[measure (mathematics)|measure]]s, over a [[metric space]] ''D''.
Informally, if the distributions are interpreted as two different ways of piling up [[Soil|earth]] (dirt) over ''D'', the EMD captures the minimum cost of building the smaller pile using dirt taken from the larger, where cost is defined as the amount of dirt moved multiplied by the distance over which it is moved.

Over probability distributions, the earth mover's distance is also known as the [[Wasserstein metric]] <math>W_1</math>, [[Leonid Kantorovich|Kantorovich]]–[[Gennadii Rubinstein|Rubinstein]] metric, or [[Colin Lingwood Mallows|Mallows]]'s distance.<ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1214/aoms/1177692631 | author = C. L. Mallows | title = A note on asymptotic joint normality | journal = Annals of Mathematical Statistics | volume = 43 | issue = 2 | pages = 508–515 | year = 1972| doi-access = free }}</ref> It is the solution of the [[optimal transport problem]], which in turn is also known as the [[Gaspard Monge|Monge]]-[[Leonid Kantorovich|Kantorovich]] problem, or sometimes the [[Frank Lauren Hitchcock|Hitchcock]]–[[Tjalling Koopmans|Koopmans]] transportation problem;<ref name="RaoRao2009">{{cite book|author1=Singiresu S. Rao|title=Engineering Optimization: Theory and Practice|year=2009|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-0-470-18352-6|page=221|edition=4th}}</ref> when the measures are uniform over a set of discrete elements, the same optimization problem is known as [[Minimum-cost flow problem#Minimum weight bipartite matching| minimum weight bipartite matching]].

==Formal definitions==
The EMD between probability distributions <math display="inline">P</math> and <math display="inline">Q</math> can be defined as an [[Infimum and supremum|infimum]] over joint probabilities:

:<math>\text{EMD}(P,Q) = \inf\limits_{\gamma \in \Pi(P, Q)} \mathbb{E}_{(x, y) \sim \gamma}\left[d(x, y)\right]\,</math>

where <math>\Pi(P, Q)</math> is the set of all [[Joint probability distribution|joint distributions]] whose [[Marginal distribution|marginals]] are <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math>.

By [[Kantorovich-Rubinstein theorem|Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality]], this can also be expressed as:

:<math>\text{EMD}(P,Q) = \sup\limits_{\| f \|_L \leq 1} \, \mathbb{E}_{x \sim P}[f(x)] - \mathbb{E}_{y \sim Q}[f(y)]\,</math>

where the supremum is taken over all [[Lipschitz continuity|1-Lipschitz continuous]] functions, i.e. <math>\| \nabla f(x)\| \leq 1 \quad \forall x</math>.

=== EMD between signatures ===

In some applications, it is convenient to represent a distribution <math display="inline">P</math> as a ''signature'', or a collection of ''clusters'', where the <math display="inline">i</math>-th cluster represents a [[feature (machine learning)|feature]] of mass <math display="inline">w_{i}</math> centered at <math display="inline">p_i </math>. 
In this formulation, consider signatures <math display="inline">P=\{(p_1,w_{p1}),(p_2,w_{p2}),...,(p_m,w_{pm})\} </math> and <math display="inline">Q=\{(q_1,w_{q1}),(q_2,w_{q2}),...,(q_n,w_{qn})\}</math>. Let <math display="inline">D=[d_{i,j}] </math> be the ground distance between clusters <math display="inline">p_i </math> and <math display="inline">q_j </math>. Then the EMD between <math display="inline">P</math> and <math display="inline">Q</math> is given by the optimal flow <math display="inline">F=[f_{i,j}] </math>, with <math display="inline">f_{i,j} </math> the flow between <math display="inline">p_i </math> and <math display="inline">q_j </math>, that minimizes the overall cost.

:<math>\min\limits_F {\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n f_{i,j}d_{i,j}}</math>

subject to the constraints:

:<math>f_{i,j}\ge0,    1\le i \le m, 1\le j \le n
</math>

:<math>\sum_{j=1}^n {f_{i,j}} \le w_{pi}, 1 \le i \le m</math>

:<math>\sum_{i=1}^m {f_{i,j}} \le w_{qj}, 1 \le j \le n</math>

:<math>\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n f_{i,j} = \min \left\{ \ \sum_{i=1}^m w_{pi}, \quad \sum_{j=1}^n w_{q j} \ \right\}</math>

The optimal flow <math display="inline">F </math> is found by solving this linear optimization problem. The earth mover's distance is defined as the work normalized by the total flow: 
:<math>\text{EMD}(P,Q) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=1}^n f_{i,j}d_{i,j}}{\sum_{i=1}^m \sum_{j=1}^n f_{i,j}}</math>

==Variants and extensions==

=== Unequal probability mass ===

Some applications may require the comparison of distributions with different total masses.  One approach is to allow for ''partial matching'',<ref name = RTG98/> where dirt from the more massive distribution is rearranged to make the less massive, and any leftover "dirt" is discarded at no cost. 
Formally, let <math display="inline">w_P</math> be the total weight of <math display="inline">P</math>, and <math display="inline">w_Q</math> be the total weight of <math display="inline">Q</math>. We have:

:<math>\text{EMD}(P,Q) = \tfrac{1}{\min(w_P, w_Q)} \inf\limits_{\gamma \in \Pi_\geq(P, Q)} \int d(x,y) \, \mathrm{d} \gamma(x,y)</math>

where <math>\Pi_\geq(P, Q)</math> is the set of all measures whose projections are <math>\geq P</math> and <math>\geq Q</math>.
Note that this generalization of EMD is not a [[metric (mathematics)|true distance]] between distributions, as it does not satisfy the triangle inequality.

An alternative approach is to allow for mass to be created or destroyed, on a global or local level, as an alternative to transportation, but with a cost penalty. In that case one must specify a real parameter <math>\alpha</math>, the ratio between the cost of creating or destroying one unit of "dirt", and the cost of transporting it by a unit distance. This is equivalent to minimizing the sum of the earth moving cost plus <math>\alpha</math> times the ''L''<sup>1</sup> distance between the rearranged pile and the second distribution. The resulting measure <math>\widehat{EMD}_\alpha</math> is a true distance function.<ref name="PeleWerman2008">{{cite book | last1 = Pele | first1 = Ofir | last2 = Werman | first2 = Michael | title = Computer Vision – ECCV 2008 | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science | chapter = A Linear Time Histogram Metric for Improved SIFT Matching | date = 2008 | volume = 5304 | pages = 495–508 | publisher = Springer Berlin Heidelberg | issn = 0302-9743 | eissn = 1611-3349 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-540-88690-7_37 | isbn = 978-3-540-88689-1 | url = }}</ref>

=== More than two distributions === 

The EMD can be extended naturally to the case where more than two distributions are compared. In this case, the "distance" between the many distributions is defined as the optimal value of a linear program. This generalized EMD may be computed exactly using a greedy algorithm, and the resulting functional has been shown to be [[Minkowski addition|Minkowski additive]] and convex monotone.<ref>{{cite journal | journal = Discrete Applied Mathematics | title = Properties of the d-dimensional earth mover's problem | last1 = Kline | first1 = Jeffery | volume = 265 | year = 2019 | pages = 128–141 | doi = 10.1016/j.dam.2019.02.042| s2cid = 127962240 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

==Computing the EMD==
The EMD can be computed by solving an instance of [[transportation problem]], using any algorithm for [[minimum-cost flow problem]], e.g. the [[network simplex algorithm]].

The [[Hungarian algorithm]] can be used to get the solution if the domain ''D'' is the set {0, 1}. If the domain is integral, it can be translated for the same algorithm by representing integral bins as multiple binary bins.

As a special case, if ''D'' is a one-dimensional array of "bins" of length ''n'', the EMD can be efficiently computed by scanning the array and keeping track of how much dirt needs to be transported between consecutive bins. Here the bins are [[zero-indexed]]:

: <math>
\begin{align}
\text{EMD}_0 &= 0 \\
\text{EMD}_{i+1} &= P_i + \text{EMD}_i - Q_i \\
\text{Total Distance} &= \sum_{i=0}^{n}|\text{EMD}_i|
\end{align}
</math>

==EMD-based similarity analysis==
EMD-based similarity analysis (EMDSA) is an important and effective tool in many [[multimedia information retrieval]]<ref name=edge>{{cite journal | author = Mark A. Ruzon |author2=Carlo Tomasi | title = Edge, Junction, and Corner Detection Using Color Distributions | journal = IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence | year = 2001 |volume=23 |issue=11 |page=1281 |doi=10.1109/34.969118 |bibcode=2001ITPAM..23.1281R }}</ref> and [[pattern recognition]]<ref name=contour>{{cite journal | author = Kristen Grauman |author2=Trevor Darrel | title = Fast contour matching using approximate earth mover's distance | journal = Proceedings of CVPR 2004 | year = 2004}}</ref> applications. However, the computational cost of EMD is super-cubic to the number of the "bins" given an arbitrary "D". Efficient and scalable EMD computation techniques for large scale data have been investigated using [[MapReduce]],<ref name=melody>{{cite conference | author =Jin Huang  |author2=Rui Zhang |author3=Rajkumar Buyya |author4=Jian Chen | title = MELODY-Join: Efficient Earth Mover's Distance Similarity Joins Using MapReduce | book-title = Proceedings of IEEE International Conference on Data Engineering | year = 2014}}</ref><ref name=mapreduce>{{cite journal | author = Jia Xu  |author2=Bin Lei |author3=Yu Gu |author4=Winslett, M. |author5=Ge Yu |author6=Zhenjie Zhang | title = Efficient Similarity Join Based on Earth Mover's Distance Using MapReduce | journal = IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering | year = 2015 |volume=27 |issue=8 |page=2148 |doi=10.1109/TKDE.2015.2411281 |bibcode=2015ITKDE..27.2148X }}</ref> as well as [[bulk synchronous parallel]] and [[resilient distributed dataset]].<ref name=bsprdd>{{cite journal | author = Jin Huang  |author2=Rui Zhang |author3=Rajkumar Buyya |author4=Jian Chen, M. |author5=Yongwei Wu | title = Heads-Join: Efficient Earth Mover's Distance Join on Hadoop | journal = IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems | year = 2015}}</ref>

==Applications==
An early application of the EMD in computer science was to compare two [[grayscale]] images that may differ due to [[dithering]], blurring, or local deformations.<ref name=peleg>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1109/34.192468 | author = S. Peleg |author2=M. Werman |author3=H. Rom  | year = 1989 | title = A unified approach to the change of resolution: Space and gray-level | journal = IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence | volume =11 | issue = 7 | pages = 739–742| s2cid = 18415340 }}</ref>  In this case, the region is the image's domain, and the total amount of light (or ink) is the "dirt" to be rearranged.

The EMD is widely used in [[content-based image retrieval]] to compute distances between the [[color histogram]]s of two [[digital image]]s.{{Citation needed|date=January 2017}}  In this case, the region is the [[RGB color model|RGB color cube]], and each image pixel is a parcel of "dirt".  The same technique can be used for any other quantitative [[pixel]] attribute, such as [[luminance]], [[image gradient|gradient]], [[optical flow|apparent motion]] in a [[video frame]], etc..

More generally, the EMD is used in [[pattern recognition]] to compare generic summaries or surrogates of data records called [[signature (patern recognition)|signatures]].<ref name = RTG98/>  A typical signature consists of list of pairs ((''x''<sub>1</sub>,''m''<sub>1</sub>), ... (''x''<sub>''n''</sub>,''m''<sub>''n''</sub>)), where each ''x''<sub>''i''</sub> is a certain "feature" (e.g., color in an image, letter in a text, etc.), and ''m''<sub>''i''</sub> is "mass" (how many times that feature occurs in the record).  Alternatively, ''x''<sub>''i''</sub> may be the [[centroid]] of a [[cluster analysis|data cluster]], and ''m''<sub>''i''</sub> the number of entities in that cluster. To compare two such signatures with the EMD, one must define a distance between features, which is interpreted as the cost of turning a unit mass of one feature into a unit mass of the other. The EMD between two signatures is then the minimum cost of turning one of them into the other.

EMD analysis has been used for quantitating multivariate changes in [[biomarkers]] measured by [[flow cytometry bioinformatics|flow cytometry]], with potential applications to other technologies that report distributions of measurements.<ref name="Orlova_2016">{{cite journal |last1=Orlova |first1=DY |last2=Zimmerman |first2=N |last3=Meehan |first3=C |last4=Meehan |first4=S |last5=Waters |first5=J |last6=Ghosn |first6=EEB |title=Earth Mover's Distance (EMD): A True Metric for Comparing Biomarker Expression Levels in Cell Populations |journal=[[PLOS One]] |date=23 March 2016 |volume=11 |issue=3 |article-number=e0151859 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0151859 |pmid=27008164 |pmc=4805242 |bibcode=2016PLoSO..1151859O |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==History==
The concept was first introduced by [[Gaspard Monge]] in 1781,<ref>{{cite journal | title = Mémoire sur la théorie des déblais et des remblais | journal = Histoire de l'Académie Royale des Science, Année 1781, avec les Mémoires de Mathématique et de Physique | year = 1781}}</ref> in the context of [[transportation theory (mathematics)|transportation theory]]. The use of the EMD as a distance measure for monochromatic images was described in 1989 by S. Peleg, M. Werman and H. Rom.<ref name=peleg/> The name "earth mover's distance" was proposed by [[Jorge Stolfi|J. Stolfi]] in 1994,<ref>J. Stolfi, personal communication to L. J. Guibas, 1994, as cited by {{cite journal
 | last1 = Rubner | first1 = Yossi
 | last2 = Tomasi | first2 = Carlo
 | last3 = Guibas | first3 = Leonidas J.
 | doi = 10.1023/A:1026543900054
 | issue = 2
 | journal = International Journal of Computer Vision
 | pages = 99–121
 | title = The earth mover's distance as a metric for image retrieval
 | url = http://robotics.stanford.edu/~rubner/papers/rubnerIjcv00.pdf
 | volume = 40
 | year = 2000| s2cid = 14106275
 }}</ref> and was used in print in 1998 by Y. Rubner, C. Tomasi and [[Leonidas J. Guibas|L. G. Guibas]].<ref name = RTG98/>
